source.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders with Board Game Models

record.file_problem: None noted; the supplied post text is readable and not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE feature-recovery evaluations to ChessGPT and OthelloGPT, a board-game setting, and reports results relevant to indirect evidence for SAE-recoverable features.
record.gate_note: The post evaluates SAE recovery of board-state information in board-game models. It does not test superposition geometry, a sparsity-dependent transition, capacity competition, or whether features are one-dimensional. Several referenced tables and plots are not present as readable numerical results in the supplied text; only the results stated in prose are recorded.
record.test_reason: Trains SAEs on ChessGPT and OthelloGPT, which have a measurable ground-truth board state. It checks whether SAE features recover that state, against randomly initialised models and linear probes. This bears on V4, whether SAEs recover sparse features in real transformers, in a board-game setting. It also bears on V5 completeness, since SAEs fall short of probes. The main aim is an evaluation method plus p-annealing, but the recovery results are reported against baselines, so this is not T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors' main contributions are two new SAE metrics (coverage, board reconstruction) that reveal differences between training methods hidden by proxy metrics, and p-annealing, which tends to score best. SAEs capture a substantial fraction of board state (F1 0.85 chess, 0.95 Othello) but fall short of linear probes, possibly missing some of it. The authors caution that board-game lessons may not transfer to language models and that the metrics may not match the model's true features.
record.recipe_differences: The post evaluates SAE feature coverage and board reconstruction in board-game models; it does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Board-state recovery varies across layers and properties; the layer-1 F1 changes from 0.01 to 0.52 when initial piece locations are included. Feature precision examples vary with activation threshold. The post also notes that layer-6 hyperparameters may not be optimal for other layers.
record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The post says its metrics may not correspond to the model's true ground-truth features, and that the maximum coverage score is unclear. Board-game results may not transfer to language models. SAE reconstruction is below linear probes, and some high-level board properties reconstruct poorly. No uncertainty estimates are stated. Referenced coverage and comparison plots/tables do not provide readable individual numeric results in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: The post references coverage tables and Pareto plots comparing SAE training methods, but their individual numeric results are not included in the supplied text. No rows were created for those unavailable values. The MLP-activation comparisons are described qualitatively but do not test whether features are spread across neurons or recovered as SAE features.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, geometry, or sparsity transition.
All: no capacity competition or importance-based allocation.
All: no test of other causes of polysemantic neurons.
Natural-language LLMs; whether features are spread across many neurons (only a qualitative MLP comparison).
Stability across seeds, and whether features are canonical. Only completeness against probes is tested, plus qualitative dependence on training method.
All: no test of feature dimensionality.

missing.what: Linear-probe baseline values per game at layer 6 (chess probe 0.99, or 0.98 with masking, per the appendix; Othello in table), needed as the comparison for r3/r4.
missing.locator: Board Reconstruction table; Appendix: Implementation details

missing.what: Random-init SAE baseline values and layer-6 MLP-neuron baseline values for coverage and reconstruction. The text says OthelloGPT MLP neurons perform 'quite well', suggesting some board state is neuron-aligned rather than superposed.
Comparison of SAE training methods (standard, gated, p-annealing, TopK) showing coverage differences invisible on proxy metrics. Feature quality depends on training method and expansion factor.
Per-layer trend: board information per layer matches across probes, SAEs and MLP activations. The layer-3 chess SAE had under 100 alive features.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong summary of arXiv:2408.00113. The tables and plots are not readable in the text, so the verdicts rest on prose statements. Rows r7-r13 are illustrations or metric controls and are relinked to none. The commenter suggests feature 172 may track an opening rather than piece squares.

versions.untested_parts: No test of overlapping or nearly orthogonal directions, feature-count-versus-dimension pressure, sparsity transitions, or regular geometry.
No test of polysemanticity, limited-capacity competition, or importance-dependent feature allocation.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.

Tests SAE recovery of board-state information in ChessGPT and OthelloGPT, not broad natural-language LLMs; does not measure features spread across neurons or compare SAE features with superposition directions.
No test of SAE features as complete, stable, or canonical units.
No test of whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: ChessGPT
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE coverage of low-level chess Board State Properties at layer 6.
rows.baseline: SAEs trained on a version with randomly initialized weights
rows.value: SAEs on the trained model substantially outperform the random-model baseline; numerical scores not stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: The post describes the result for trained-model SAEs; the referenced coverage table's individual values are not available in the supplied text.

rows.subject: OthelloGPT
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE coverage of low-level Othello Board State Properties at layer 6.
rows.baseline: SAEs trained on a version with randomly initialized weights
rows.value: SAEs on the trained model substantially outperform the random-model baseline; numerical scores not stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: The post separately notes that OthelloGPT MLP activations also perform quite well, but gives no numerical coverage value for them.

rows.subject: ChessGPT
rows.operation_detail: Measured maximum board-reconstruction F1 from SAEs trained on layer 6.
rows.locator: Key Results; Sparse Autoencoder Board Reconstruction Metric
rows.note: The post says the best score across SAEs trained on layer 6 was reported, and that SAE performance did not reach that of linear probes.
rows.check: For V4 this is observed: SAEs recover a substantial fraction of board state (F1 0.85), well above the random-model SAEs. For V5 it is partial, because performance is below linear probes; the record's 'partial' fits V5, not V4. The baseline should be the linear probe (chess probe F1 0.98 with masking, per the appendix) and the random-init SAE, not 'not stated'. The value is the best of many SAEs at layer 6, so it is a selected maximum.

rows.subject: OthelloGPT
rows.operation_detail: Measured maximum board-reconstruction F1 from SAEs trained on layer 6.
rows.locator: Key Results; Sparse Autoencoder Board Reconstruction Metric
rows.note: The post says the best score across SAEs trained on layer 6 was reported, and that SAE performance did not reach that of linear probes.
rows.check: Same as r3: observed for V4 (F1 0.95, above the random baseline), partial for V5 (below linear probes). The baseline should be the linear probe and random-init SAE. The Othello probe value is in a table the text does not include. The value is a selected maximum across SAEs.

rows.subject: ChessGPT
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE reconstruction of the high-level chess property that an en passant capture is available.
rows.note: Reported as an example of a high-level chess board-state feature the approach reconstructs well.

rows.subject: ChessGPT
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE reconstruction of the high-level chess property that a pinned piece is on the board.
rows.note: Reported as an example of a high-level board-state feature the approach reconstructs less well.
rows.check: Pinned-piece F1 is 0.20. The authors say it is unclear whether ChessGPT internally represents such high-level concepts. A low score therefore cannot separate SAE failure from the model lacking the feature.

rows.measure: Probability that a White Knight is on F3 when the feature is active

rows.operation_detail: Checked whether the feature classified any black-pawn square state with high precision.
rows.measure: High-precision classification of black pawn locations
rows.value: Not high precision for any square
rows.note: A qualitative result for the feature example; the associated model is not explicitly named.

rows.subject: ChessGPT
rows.operation_detail: Measured board reconstruction from an SAE trained on residual-stream activations after layer 1, excluding pieces on their initial starting locations.
rows.note: The text says this layer contains very little board-state information as measured by linear probes.
rows.check: A metric-design control. Layer 1 carries almost no board information per probes, so a low F1 is expected and says nothing against V4.

rows.subject: ChessGPT
rows.operation_detail: Measured board reconstruction from an SAE trained on residual-stream activations after layer 1, including pieces on their initial starting locations.
rows.baseline: 0.01 when initial piece locations are excluded
rows.note: The post attributes the increase to the board being mostly reconstructible early in games from token position in the PGN string.
rows.check: A control showing that the PGN-position confound inflates F1 when starting squares are counted. It is a methodological check, not a result on V4.

relationships.condition: ChessGPT and OthelloGPT, layer-6 residual-stream SAEs, low-level board-state properties and en passant
relationships.reason: SAE features recover board state well above random-init SAE baselines on coverage and reconstruction (F1 0.85/0.95; en passant 0.92) (r1-r5).
relationships.display_finding: SAE features beat random-initialization SAE baselines on coverage and reconstruction, with F1 of 0.85 and 0.95, and 0.92 for en passant.

relationships.condition: ChessGPT and OthelloGPT layer 6, best SAE versus linear probe
relationships.reason: The best SAEs reconstruct board state below linear probes (0.85/0.95 vs probe ~0.98-0.99); the authors say SAEs may not capture all of it. Metric scores also vary by training method and expansion factor (text) (r3, r4).
relationships.display_finding: The best SAEs reached 0.85 and 0.95 on board-state reconstruction against about 0.98–0.99 for linear probes, and scores varied with training method and expansion factor.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The SAEs recover board-state information, including board-reconstruction F1 scores of 0.85 and 0.95 and high-precision feature examples (r3-r10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Board reconstruction is incomplete or varies by property, activation threshold, and layer-1 board-position setup
reader_labels.reason: Scores are below the linear-probe performance, some property recovery is weak, and layer-1 reconstruction changes substantially when initial positions are included (r6, r9, r11-r13).
